label: sequence started with p: late original-phase steps and <DEL>
explanation: Fires when the first original token is p (first_tok=p carries 94% of activation mass, 22x lift), from step 4 of the original phase through the <DEL> step. It does not depend on the current input token, and it is silent at t=0-3 and for the whole copy phase (one activation in total). Activation grows over the original phase, peaks around steps 5-8 just before the delimiter, and is slightly lower at <DEL>. The strongest examples all start with "p p". Weak residual firing (about 7% of mass) shows up when p is the second token or the first token is r, and on other sequences at near-zero levels. Steps the predicate misses are almost all in the lowest activation quartile. Its false positives are mostly step 4 in sequences where another p follows soon after the first.

issues: The claims check out, so this is not a refutation. Test scores reproduce the reported numbers: P 0.985, R 0.695, F1 0.815, mass recall 0.938, correlation 0.93.

Recall is low (0.695) because of near-zero diffuse firing, not because the predicate misses a class. By activation quartile the predicate covers 3.9%, 74%, 100% and 100% of active steps, and the missed steps hold only about 6% of activation mass. Test misses show sequences that do not start with p, firing at 0.01-0.1 of max with no consistent token, position or length pattern.
Copy-phase silence holds: (orig(0)==p) & (phase==2) gives precision 0, and over the whole dev split the copy phase has 1 active step.
Silence at t=0-3 mostly holds: t=0-2 have zero activations and t=3 has 0.6% of steps active with 1.1% of mass. (orig(0)==p) & (t==3) has precision 0.19, so it is right to exclude t=3.

The residual-firing claims are accurate and small. orig(1)==p (with first token not p) has precision 0.09 and 3.6% of mass. First token r at t>=4 has precision 0.11 and 1.5% of mass. Adding either to the predicate lowers F1 (adding orig(1)==p gives F1 0.698).

The false-positive class is real but small, and the explanation already states it: 844 test steps, mostly t=4 where another p appears at position 2-3, which delays the onset by a step. Excluding those cases raises precision to 0.999 but lowers F1 (0.78-0.80), so the original predicate is the better trade-off.
The profile supports the peak and onset claims. Mass share by t is highest at 5-6 (0.247 and 0.236), t=4 has 0.175, and the delimiter step has 24% of mass. The top examples all start with 'p p'.
